questions.question: Which hypotheses are required in the Mean Value Theorem for a function $f\colon [a,b]\to \mathbb{R}$?
options: Differentiability on $[a,b]$ and continuity only at $a$
Continuity on $(a,b)$ with no differentiability condition
Differentiability only at the endpoints $a$ and $b$
questions.explanation: The MVT requires $f$ continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a,b)$.
questions.source_support: The theorem statement lists continuity on $[a,b]$ and differentiability on $(a,b)$.

option_explanations: Differentiability on the whole $[a,b]$ is not required (only on the open $(a,b)$), and continuity only at $a$ is far too weak; the theorem needs continuity on all of $[a,b]$.
Interior continuity without differentiability is insufficient; the MVT needs differentiability on $(a,b)$ to form $f'(c)$.
Endpoint derivatives alone give no interior slope; the theorem needs $f$ differentiable at every interior point $c\in(a,b)$.

questions.question: In what sense does the Mean Value Theorem generalise Rolle's theorem?
options: It removes the need for differentiability on $(a,b)$
It applies only to constant functions
It allows the average rate $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ to be nonzero
questions.explanation: Rolle's theorem is the special case of the MVT with $f(a)=f(b)$ (zero secant slope, giving $f'(c)=0$); the MVT generalises it by allowing a non-zero average rate $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
questions.source_support: The theorem generalises Rolle's theorem.

The derivative $f'(c)$ need not be zero; the MVT gives $f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, which is generally non-zero (e.g. $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$ gives $f'(c)=1$).
The MVT applies to nonconstant functions, not only constant ones; e.g. $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$ is nonconstant and satisfies the MVT.
